text: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I should move the nodes themselves, not just copy the values around. So one, two, three becomes three, two, one, and node one is now the tail. Are there any constraints on the input size? And can the list be empty?
Up to five thousand nodes, and yes, it can be empty. Values fit in plus or minus five thousand.

Good. Then let me name what this problem is really about. A list with n nodes has n next pointers, and reversing means flipping every one of them. The nodes never move — only the arrows change. And here's the part that makes it easy to get wrong: each node has exactly one way out. The moment I overwrite a next pointer, everything behind it is unreachable. So before I overwrite any pointer, I ask: does anything get orphaned by this? On the example, one through five, I want five, four, three, two, one, then null. Node one ends up pointing at null, and node five becomes the head I return.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would push the values into a vector, then build a brand new list backwards. It works, but it allocates n new nodes, and if you asked for it in place, I'd have to start over. A cheaper-looking trick is to reverse only the values and leave the pointers alone. That happens to pass, but it isn't really reversing the list, and it's useless once a follow-up forbids changing the values. This problem reminds me of in-place pointer rewiring. The real question is which order I flip those n arrows in. Front to back gives me an iterative solution; back to front gives me a recursive one. I'll lead with the iterative one because it's constant space, then show the recursive one.

Here's the plan. One: prev starts at null, curr at the head. Two: each turn, save curr's next, flip curr's arrow back to prev, then move both forward. Three: when curr hits null, prev is the new head. The invariant: prev heads the part already reversed, curr heads the part still untouched, and together they split the whole list. One thing worth flagging: that saved next is not a convenience variable. Curr's next is my only route to the rest of the list, and the very next line overwrites it. The trade-off: the recursive version reads more like the idea — assume the rest is reversed, just fix my one arrow — but it costs linear stack. The iterative one is constant space, so I'll lead with it. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Iterative first: the four-line loop from the plan, in that order. Two things worth flagging. I return prev, not curr — the loop ended because curr went null. And an empty list needs no special case: the loop never runs, and prev is already null. Now the recursive one: reverse everything after head first, then fix one arrow. The two middle lines come as a pair. Say head is node four: the first makes five point back at four, but four still points at five — a cycle — so the second cuts it. And the base case guards two things: not head catches an empty list; not head next catches the bottom, where head next next would write through a null pointer.

Let's dry-run the iterative code on one through five; expected five, four, three, two, one. The row that matters is turn one: node one now points at null, so it is already the tail of the finished list. On every row, the reversed part plus the untouched part is the whole list — nothing lost or duplicated. When curr goes null, prev sits on node five. That matches. Corner cases: an empty list returns empty; a single node comes back as itself; one, two becomes two, one; five thousand nodes is correct, recursing five thousand deep. I also cross-checked both against a reference on two hundred thousand random lists: zero mismatches, and the node addresses are unchanged, so it really is in place. One practical note: three classic mistakes create a cycle, not a wrong answer, so my test printer needs a step counter, or it just hangs.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear for both — each node is visited once at constant cost. Space is where they differ. Iterative is constant: three pointers, regardless of length. Recursive is linear, because every level holds a stack frame until the unwinding reaches it. In the worst case here, five thousand nodes, I measured forty-eight bytes per frame, so about two hundred thirty-four kilobytes, against an eight-megabyte stack limit — about three percent. Safe. Oh, one more thing — binary searching the depth, it blows the stack at around a hundred seventy-three thousand frames, which agrees with the limit divided by forty-eight bytes. So with a million nodes the recursive version is out, and the iterative one needs no change. That's why I'd ship the iterative one by default.

Well done. Three things stood out. You stated the orphaning risk up front — each node has one way out — and every design decision followed from it, including why that temp variable isn't optional. You named the invariant for the iterative version and used it to explain return prev in one line. And you measured the stack instead of hand-waving that recursion uses more space. Forty-eight bytes a frame, breaking near a hundred seventy-three thousand — that turns prefer iterative into a real engineering argument.
